title: Draw near a span
hookLine: whoever draws near Me a span, I draw near a cubit, whoever comes walking, I come running (Bukhari)

lines: A SPAN: THE HAND SPREAD WIDE.
cards: Spread your hand wide, thumb to little finger. That's a span, an old way of measuring from before tape measures. Now hold out your forearm, elbow to fingertip.
That's a cubit. Now stretch both arms out as far as they go, like you're about to hug someone. That's a fathom.
Three measures, all carried on the body. Yesterday's sacred hadith keeps going, and it uses exactly these three. Today: draw near a span.

teach.h: A SPAN, A CUBIT, A FATHOM.

teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ relates that Allah says: if My servant draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near a cubit, I draw near a fathom; and if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running.
Three measures, each bigger than the last. Second, the arithmetic. Who moves first in the sentence?
The servant, and only a little.
And the answer is never the same size as the step. It's always more. A span gets a cubit.

teach.h: TWO WAYS OF READING THE RUNNING.
teach.b: Walking gets running. Third, how scholars read the picture. Not all the same way.
Some explained the running as the speed of Allah's mercy and help, His answer reaching a person faster and fuller than the effort that reached for Him.
Others accepted the words as they come, without asking how, and without likening Allah to anything. Both readings keep the point: the response outruns the step.
The Qur'an speaks of the same nearness in its own way, in Pickthall's translation: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." Fourth, a picture from ordinary life.
A toddler takes one wobbly step toward a parent across the kitchen. The parent doesn't stand still and wait for the whole distance to be crossed. They come, fast, and scoop the child up.
So the smallest step counts. One prayer after a long gap. One honest word of repentance.
One kind act. The hadith doesn't ask for a marathon. It asks for a span.

how: Muslims recall this hadith when returning to prayer or repentance after a gap, and teachers use it to encourage small, steady steps rather than waiting to feel ready.

games.q: what does “draw near a span” mean?
o: keeping a careful distance from Allah, out of respect
the smallest step toward Allah, met by a far larger answer
measuring out a prayer space with your own hand

games.q: draw near a span — tap the pairs.

s: in the hadith, the servant has to cover most of the distance
the servant moves a span; the answer is always larger, and walking is met with running.
the hadith uses three measures: span, cubit and fathom
each bigger than the last, all carried on the body.
every scholar read the running in exactly the same way
some explained it as the speed of mercy; others accepted the words without asking how.

games.q: after a long gap, you take one small step back toward Allah. in this hadith, what comes back to meet you?
o: a step of exactly the same size.
something larger: a span answered with a cubit, walking with running.
nothing, until you've done much more.
games.why: something larger. the answer always outruns the step: a span gets a cubit, a cubit gets a fathom, walking gets running.

practice: Lay your hand flat on your knee, spread wide: a span.

Choose one small step within reach today, not a whole new life: if you pray, maybe one prayer you've been missing or a few minutes with the Qur'an; if you don't, maybe a call to someone you've drifted from, or an apology you've been carrying.
Then breathe with the hadith's picture: a step taken, and an answer running to meet it.

wordCard.voice: Draw near a span. The smallest step toward Allah, and in this sacred hadith, an answer that is always larger, coming running. Today's word.
